799.title: Broken cisterns (Jeremiah 2:13)
799.hook: they left the fountain of living waters for cisterns that hold no water
799.howItsDone: Jeremiah 2, with its broken cisterns, is read in synagogue as a haftarah in the summer weeks before Tisha b'Av, when the Prophets' words of warning are read.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a plain almond branch turned out to mean watching. Your line was the watching tree. What did you see when you looked twice? Today, Jeremiah's first great complaint, about water. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

In a dry land, rain doesn't fall all year. So people dug cisterns: pits cut into the rock to catch the rain and keep it for the dry months. A good cistern is a lifeline. A cracked one is worse than none, because you only find out when you lower the bucket and it comes up empty. Now set a spring next to that, water rising out of the ground on its own, cold and moving, free for anyone. Jeremiah puts the two side by side, in a single verse.
screen: `A PIT CUT INTO ROCK.` → `THE BUCKET COMES UP EMPTY.` → `A SPRING, FREE FOR ANYONE.`

segments.voice: Here it is. "For my people have committed two evils; they have forsaken me the fountain of living waters, and hewed them out cisterns, broken cisterns, that can hold no water." Two evils, and they're a pair. The first is leaving: walking away from the spring. The second is the work that follows: digging. Hewing a cistern out of rock is hard labor. The people aren't lazy in this picture. They're exhausted, working hard on something that leaks. And living water, in Hebrew mayim chayim, means water that moves, from a spring or a stream, as opposed to water that sits. In Jeremiah's verse, God is that spring. The broken cisterns, in the chapter around it, are the other gods and the foreign powers the people chased, even going to Egypt and Assyria to drink their rivers' water; earlier, God asks whether any nation has ever changed its gods, and says my people have changed their glory for what doesn't profit. Here's a detail worth keeping: a cistern isn't bad in itself. The Mishnah, in Pirkei Avot, praises a great student, Rabbi Eliezer, as a plastered cistern that never loses a drop: someone who keeps everything he learns. The trouble in Jeremiah isn't storing water. It's trading a spring for a container, and then a container that cracks. The rabbis also compared the words of Torah to water, reading Isaiah's call to everyone who is thirsty to come to the waters as an invitation to learn. So the question this verse leaves is a practical one: what am I working hard to fill that never stays full?
screen: `TWO EVILS, A PAIR.` · then, large: `THE FOUNTAIN OF LIVING WATERS.` · then: `A CISTERN THAT KEEPS EVERY DROP.` · `WHAT NEVER STAYS FULL?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: drop one thing that doesn't hold water. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last week. Where did your time and effort pour in, and drain right out? Maybe an app you refresh, an argument you keep rehearsing, a purchase that was supposed to fix something. Pick one. No need to judge yourself; just see it clearly, the way you'd see a crack in a bucket. Then decide one small way to step back from it today: an hour without it, a day without it. And let one living thing take its place: a walk, a call, a page of learning. The bell holds the time.
Broken cisterns. Pits dug with great effort that can hold no water, set beside the spring the people walked away from. Today's word.
Your line: broken cisterns. Today, when you catch yourself refilling something that always drains, name it quietly: broken cistern. Day seven hundred ninety-nine.

800.title: Is there no balm? (Jeremiah 8:22)
800.hook: "Is there no balm in Gilead?" the prophet weeps for his people's hurt
800.howItsDone: Jeremiah 8 and 9 are read in synagogue as the haftarah on the morning of Tisha b'Av, the fast day of mourning, when Lamentations is also read aloud.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the people left a flowing spring and dug cisterns that leak. Your line was broken cisterns. Did you catch one? Today the prophet who warned them starts to weep for them. Day eight hundred.

"Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there?" To hear the sting in that question, you need to know what Gilead meant. In the book of Genesis, Joseph's brothers, about to sell him, look up and see a caravan of Ishmaelites coming from Gilead, their camels bearing spicery and balm and myrrh, going down to Egypt. In that story, Gilead is where the balm comes from. So Jeremiah's question is like standing in a pharmacy and asking: is there no medicine here? Of course there is. That's what makes it hurt.
screen: `IS THERE NO BALM IN GILEAD?` → `A CARAVAN FROM GILEAD.` → `MEDICINE IN THE PHARMACY.`

segments.voice: Listen to the verses just before. "The harvest is past, the summer is ended, and we are not saved." The season for gathering has come and gone, and nothing was gathered in. Then Jeremiah's own voice breaks through: "For the hurt of the daughter of my people am I hurt." This is the man who has spent chapter after chapter warning, accusing, calling the people back from broken cisterns. And here he isn't standing above them. Their wound is his wound. Then the question: "Is there no balm in Gilead; is there no physician there? why then is not the health of the daughter of my people recovered?" Notice the shape of it. The question doesn't doubt that healing exists. The balm is real; the physician is there. What baffles him is the gap between the cure and the patient. And the verse doesn't answer. It stays a question. Right after it, Jeremiah wishes his head were waters and his eyes a fountain of tears, so he could weep day and night for his people. Tradition says Jeremiah also wrote the book of Lamentations, and the Talmud records that view. Whether or not you read it that way, here is a prophet whose anger and grief live in the same chest. That pairing reaches past his own day. There is a particular pain in watching help exist and still not reach: the friend who won't call the doctor, the family that won't talk. Jeremiah doesn't fix it. He stays, and he hurts with them.
screen: `THE HARVEST IS PAST.` · then, large: `FOR THE HURT OF MY PEOPLE AM I HURT.` · then: `THE CURE IS REAL. WHY NO HEALING?` · `ANGER AND GRIEF IN ONE CHEST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: care for someone who is hurting. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who is in pain right now, in body or in spirit. Maybe help exists for them and hasn't reached them yet. Don't try to solve it in the next two minutes. Just let their hurt sit next to you for a moment, the way Jeremiah let his people's hurt be his own. Then choose one small act of care for today: a message, a meal, an offer to sit with them, a ride to an appointment. Something that carries a little balm the last few steps. The bell holds the time.
Is there no balm? Jeremiah's cry: the cure is in Gilead, so why are my people not healed? Today's word.
Your line: is there no balm. Today, carry a little balm to one person who's hurting, even if all you bring is your presence. Day eight hundred.

801.title: Glory in kindness (Jeremiah 9:22–23)
801.hook: let no one glory in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the God of kindness and justice
801.howItsDone: These verses close the haftarah read in synagogue on the morning of Tisha b'Av, so the day of mourning's reading from the Prophets ends on kindness, justice and righteousness.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah asked why there was no healing when the balm was right there in Gilead. Your line was is there no balm. Who did you bring a little to? Today, a few verses on, the same prophet talks about bragging. Day eight hundred one.

Scroll any feed for a minute and the boasts sort themselves into three piles. Look how smart I am: the degree, the hot take, the clever reply. Look how strong I am: the workout, the win, the promotion. Look how much I have: the car, the kitchen, the trip. The piles have changed their clothes over the centuries, but not their shape. Jeremiah names all three in one breath, and then tells you the one thing worth boasting about. It isn't any of them.
screen: `SMART, STRONG, RICH.` → `THE BOASTS HAVEN'T CHANGED.` → `ONE THING WORTH BOASTING ABOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the verse. "Thus saith the LORD, Let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, neither let the mighty man glory in his might, let not the rich man glory in his riches." Wisdom, might, riches: the three piles. Notice that the verse doesn't say they're bad. Being wise is good; being strong is useful; money can do a lot. It only says they're not what to glory in. Then the turn. "But let him that glorieth glory in this, that he understandeth and knoweth me, that I am the LORD which exercise lovingkindness, judgment, and righteousness, in the earth: for in these things I delight, saith the LORD." Three Hebrew words: chesed, kindness; mishpat, justice; tzedakah, righteousness. Three boasts out; three of God's ways in. And look at the strange shape of the boast. It isn't I am kind. It's I know a God who does kindness. To know God, in this verse, is to understand what God does and delights in. And where? In the earth. Not only in heaven, but here, in kitchens and courts and streets. In the last chapter of his Guide for the Perplexed, the philosopher Maimonides turns to this very verse. His reading, in brief: knowing God leads somewhere practical, to acting with kindness, justice and righteousness yourself. So the verse that starts as a ban on bragging ends, in Maimonides' reading, as a job description: the one boast it allows is knowing what God delights in, and that knowing is meant to show in the hands.
screen: `NOT WISDOM, NOT MIGHT, NOT RICHES.` · then, large: `KINDNESS, JUSTICE, RIGHTEOUSNESS.` · then: `IN THE EARTH.` · `MAIMONIDES' LAST CHAPTER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: boast only of a kindness. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days. Find one moment of kindness you saw, or were given, or managed to give. Someone held a door, covered a shift, said the right word. Hold it for a moment, and let it be the thing that matters about your week. If it was someone else's kindness, plan to tell someone about it today, out loud, with their name. Jeremiah's verse allows one boast, knowing the God who delights in kindness; telling someone else's kindness is a small way of pointing to it. If you pray, you can hold his words: for in these things I delight. The bell holds the time.
Glory in kindness. Not in wisdom, might or riches, but in knowing the God who does kindness, justice and righteousness in the earth. Today's word.
Your line: glory in kindness. Today, if you catch yourself about to show off, tell a story about someone's kindness instead. Day eight hundred one.

802.title: The potter's house (Jeremiah 18:1–6)
802.hook: clay spoiled on the wheel is shaped again
802.howItsDone: On Yom Kippur evening, Ashkenazi prayer books include the liturgical poem Ki hineh kachomer, behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, which takes its image from Jeremiah 18.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah threw out wisdom, might and riches as things to brag about, and kept kindness. Your line was glory in kindness. Whose kindness did you tell? Today, the prophet goes to work, in someone else's workshop. Day eight hundred two.

"Arise, and go down to the potter's house, and there I will cause thee to hear my words." This time the message doesn't come in a vision or a dream. Jeremiah is sent on an errand, down to a workshop. He goes, and there's the potter, working a lump of clay at the wheel. Wet hands, a turning wheel, a pot rising. And then, halfway up, something goes wrong. In a pottery class it looks like this: a wobble, a slump, a wall caving in. What the potter does next is the whole lesson.
screen: `GO DOWN TO THE POTTER'S HOUSE.` → `A POT RISING ON THE WHEEL.` → `SOMETHING GOES WRONG.`

segments.voice: Here's what Jeremiah sees. "And the vessel that he made of clay was marred in the hand of the potter: so he made it again another vessel, as seemed good to the potter to make it." Look at what he doesn't do. He doesn't throw the clay out. He doesn't sweep it off the wheel into the trash. The spoiled pot is still soft clay, and soft clay can be pressed back down and raised again into something else. Then the word comes. "O house of Israel, cannot I do with you as this potter?" And: "Behold, as the clay is in the potter's hand, so are ye in mine hand." On its own, that line could sound like a threat: you're just clay, and I can crush you. But read on, into the next verses. God says that if a nation he has spoken against turns from its evil, he will relent of the evil he planned for it. And if a nation he planned to build turns to evil, the plan can change too. The potter image is about turning. A vessel that's still on the wheel isn't finished. Mistakes don't end it; they're the reason the potter's hands go back to work. Jewish tradition carries this picture into Yom Kippur. In the Ashkenazi evening service, a liturgical poem built on Jeremiah's image is sung: behold, as clay in the hand of the potter, so are we in your hand. On the night of turning, the people call themselves clay that can still be reshaped.
screen: `THE VESSEL WAS MARRED.` · `HE MADE IT AGAIN.` · then, large: `AS CLAY IN THE POTTER'S HAND.` · then: `CLAY ON THE WHEEL CAN TURN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let yourself be reshaped. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one place in your life that feels marred, a habit that slumped, a plan that caved in, a way you've been treating someone. Don't throw it away in your mind, and don't defend it either. Just hold it the way a potter holds soft clay. Ask: what could this become, if it were pressed down and raised again? Let one small new shape come. Then breathe out, and let your hands, your shoulders, your jaw go soft, like clay that can still move. The bell holds the time.
The potter's house. Where Jeremiah watched a spoiled pot pressed down and made again, and heard: as clay in the potter's hand. Today's word.
Your line: as clay in his hand. Today, when something you made goes wrong, don't throw it out; press it down and try again. Day eight hundred two.

803.title: Fire in my bones (Jeremiah 20:7–9)
803.hook: Jeremiah tries to stop speaking, but the word is "as it were a burning fire shut up in my bones"
803.tomorrow: Seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4–7)
803.howItsDone: Jews read Jeremiah's complaints, like this one in chapter 20, as part of the prophetic books; arguing with God, from Abraham to Job to Jeremiah, has a recognized place in Jewish prayer and study.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a spoiled pot was pressed down and made again. Your line was as clay in his hand. Did something get a second shape? Today, the prophet tries to quit. Day eight hundred three.

Jeremiah has a bad night. Pashhur, a priest and an officer in the Temple, hears him prophesying disaster, has him struck, and locks him overnight in the stocks at the upper gate of Benjamin, by the house of the Lord. The next morning Pashhur lets him out, and Jeremiah speaks one more hard word to him. Then the book opens the door to Jeremiah's private prayer, and what comes out is a complaint against God.
screen: `A NIGHT IN THE STOCKS.` → `ONE MORE HARD WORD.` → `A COMPLAINT AGAINST GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's how it starts. "O LORD, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived: thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed: I am in derision daily, every one mocketh me." The Hebrew verb behind deceived can also mean persuaded or enticed. Translators wrestle with how strong to make it. Either way, Jeremiah is saying: you talked me into this, and I lost. Every time I open my mouth it's violence and ruin, and every time, I'm laughed at. So he makes a decision any of us might make. "Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name." Fine. I'm done. Silence. And here's what happens. "But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay." He tries holding it in, and holding it in wears him out more than the mockery did. The word won't stay buried. Two things are worth keeping. First, the book keeps this prayer. It doesn't tidy Jeremiah into a calm saint. Jewish tradition has room for arguing with God: Abraham bargains over Sodom, Job demands an answer, and here a prophet says, you tricked me. Second, the fire isn't a reward or a glow of inspiration. It's a pressure. Some truths, once you know them, cost more to keep silent than to say. Jeremiah's lesson isn't that speaking got easier. It's that silence turned out to be impossible.
screen: `THOU HAST DECEIVED ME.` · `I WILL NOT SPEAK ANY MORE.` · then, large: `A BURNING FIRE SHUT UP IN MY BONES.` · then: `SILENCE COSTS MORE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say what burns in you. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself: is there something I keep swallowing? A truth someone needs to hear, an apology I owe, a worry about someone I love, a thing that's wrong and I've stayed quiet about. Let it come up. Don't speak it to anyone yet. First, put it into one clear sentence, in your head, kind and true. Then decide who should hear it, and when. If the sentence comes out angry, breathe and try again until it's honest without being cruel. The bell holds the time.
Fire in my bones. Jeremiah tried to stop speaking, and the word burned inside him until he couldn't hold it. Today's word.
Your line: fire in my bones. Today, say the one sentence you've been swallowing, kindly, to the person who needs it. Day eight hundred three.

804.title: Seek the peace of the city (Jeremiah 29:4–7)
804.word: Seek the peace of the city
804.hook: a letter to the exiles: build houses, plant gardens, pray for the city you live in
804.carry: seek the peace of the city
804.howItsDone: In synagogue, a prayer for the welfare of the country and its government is said on Shabbat morning after the Torah reading, carrying forward Jeremiah's instruction to seek the peace of the city.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Jeremiah tried to keep quiet, and the word burned in him. Your line was fire in my bones. Did you say your sentence? Today, the prophet speaks by letter, to people far away. Day eight hundred four.

A letter goes out from Jerusalem, carried by messengers, to people who have been taken away to Babylon: elders, priests, prophets, craftsmen, ordinary families. They're living in a foreign city, the capital of the empire that conquered them. And some prophets among them are saying: don't unpack. This will be over soon. You'll be home before long. Jeremiah's letter says something else, and to people who wanted to hear go home, it is a hard letter.
screen: `A LETTER TO BABYLON.` → `DON'T UNPACK, SOME SAY.` → `JEREMIAH SAYS SOMETHING ELSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the heart of it. "Build ye houses, and dwell in them; and plant gardens, and eat the fruit of them." Houses are for staying. Gardens take time to bear. Jeremiah is telling the exiles to stop waiting at the door. Marry, he goes on, have children, see your children married, increase there, and don't dwindle. Then the line that gives us today's title. "And seek the peace of the city whither I have caused you to be carried away captives, and pray unto the LORD for it: for in the peace thereof shall ye have peace." Read it twice. The city is Babylon. These are the people who conquered Jerusalem. And the exiles are told to seek its shalom, its peace, its welfare, and to pray for it. Not because Babylon deserves it, but because their lives are now tied to it: in its peace, your peace. Later in the same chapter the letter promises a return, but not soon. Until then, the instruction is to live fully where you are. A related teaching appears in the Mishnah. Pirkei Avot records Rabbi Chanina, the deputy high priest, saying: pray for the welfare of the government, for without fear of it, people would swallow one another alive. And in synagogue prayer books, there's a prayer for the country and its government, said on Shabbat. Jeremiah's letter asked something hard of people living somewhere they never chose: plant a garden there, and pray for the place.
screen: `BUILD HOUSES, PLANT GARDENS.` · then, large: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY.` · then: `IN ITS PEACE, YOUR PEACE.` · `PRAY FOR THE WELFARE OF THE GOVERNMENT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for your town, or simply wish it well. Settle, and breathe. Bring your town or city to mind, the actual streets. The bus stop, the corner store, the school, the clinic, the park. Pick one place. Think of the people who work there, and the people who need it. Ask: what does this place's peace need right now? Fewer potholes, a kinder council meeting, a full food bank, a safe walk home. If you pray, you can hold Jeremiah's words for it: seek the peace of the city. If you don't, hold the wish. Then find one small thing to do for it this week. The bell holds the time.
Seek the peace of the city. Jeremiah's letter to the exiles in Babylon: build, plant, and pray for the city where you live, for in its peace is yours. Today's word.
screen: `SEEK THE PEACE OF THE CITY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: seek the peace of the city. Today, do one small thing for the place you live: pick up, show up, or help out. Day eight hundred four.

805.title: Rachel weeping (Jeremiah 31:14–16)
805.hook: Rachel weeps for her children, and is told "there is hope for thy future"
805.howItsDone: These verses come near the end of the haftarah read on the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and people come to pray at the site known as Rachel's Tomb, near Bethlehem.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a letter told the exiles to plant gardens in Babylon. Your line was seek the peace of the city. What did you do for your town? Today, from the chapters of comfort, a mother's voice. Day eight hundred five.

"A voice was heard in Ramah, lamentation, and bitter weeping; Rahel weeping for her children refused to be comforted for her children, because they were not." Rachel. Jacob's beloved, the wife he waited and worked for. She died on the road, giving birth to a son, and Genesis says she was buried there, in the way to Ephrath, which is Bethlehem. Generations later, Jeremiah hears her voice again. Her children are being led away into exile, and she is weeping.
screen: `A VOICE WAS HEARD IN RAMAH.` → `BURIED ON THE ROAD.` → `SHE REFUSES TO BE COMFORTED.`

segments.voice: Notice first what Rachel refuses. Comfort. Not because comfort is bad, but because her children are gone, and nothing short of their return will do. The text lets her grief stand at full height. Then God answers, and look how. He doesn't tell her she's overreacting. "Refrain thy voice from weeping, and thine eyes from tears: for thy work shall be rewarded, saith the LORD; and they shall come again from the land of the enemy." Thy work. Her weeping is called work, labor that will be paid. And then: "And there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border." The Jewish Publication Society's old translation puts it this way: "there is hope for thy future." Rabbinic tradition built on this. The commentator Rashi explains why Jacob buried Rachel on the road instead of in the family tomb: so that when her children were driven into exile, they would pass her grave, and she would come out and weep and plead for them. And a midrash in Lamentations Rabbah tells that when the Temple fell, Abraham, Isaac, Jacob and Moses each pleaded for the people, and were not answered. Then Rachel spoke, and God said: for your sake I will bring them back. So the one who refused comfort is the one whose tears are heard. Hope here isn't the opposite of grief. It's what God says to grief that refuses to quit.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: hope for someone who seems lost. Settle, and breathe. Let one person come to mind who seems far away right now: lost to addiction, to anger, to grief, to a life that's drifted off from yours. Don't argue with how hard it is. Rachel didn't. Just let yourself care about them, the way she did, without pretending. Then, quietly, set Jeremiah's words next to their name: there is hope. If you pray, you can hold them in prayer. If there's one small thing that might reach them, a message, a door left open, note it for today. The bell holds the time.
Rachel weeping. The mother of the exiles, crying for her children and refusing comfort, and told: there is hope for thy future. Today's word.

Your line: there is hope. Today, keep one door open for someone who seems lost. And look back at this week: broken cisterns, is there no balm, glory in kindness, as clay in his hand, fire in my bones, seek the peace of the city, and there is hope. Day eight hundred five.
